title: Ni'amah bin al-Rabi'a and Naomi
summary: In the city of Kufa lived a noble young gentleman named Ni'amah, whose family had raised an orphan maiden named Naomi from her childhood....
full_text:
In the city of Kufa lived a noble young gentleman named Ni'amah, whose family had raised an orphan maiden named Naomi from her childhood. As they grew into youth, Naomi mastered calligraphy, jurisprudence, and music, and their mutual affection blossomed into marriage.

The tyrannical governor of Basra, Al-Hajjaj, hearing of Naomi’s peerless gifts, sent his guards to abduct her by stealth, presenting her as a gift to the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik in Damascus. Devastated by the loss of his beloved bride, Ni'amah swore never to rest until he had found her.

Taking his purse of gold, Ni'amah rode across the Syrian desert to Damascus. He sought the counsel of a venerable physician, who advised him not to storm the royal palace with steel, but to use art and patience. Ni'amah disguised himself as a master physician's apprentice, carrying rare elixirs and a golden medicine chest.

His gentle manners and medical skill gained him entrance to the palace infirmary. One afternoon, while preparing scented pastilles in the inner courtyard, he heard a sweet voice singing from behind a silk lattice—it was Naomi, singing verses of longing for her home in Kufa!

Recognizing her voice, Ni'amah inscribed a verse of reassurance upon the back of a silk fan and had it conveyed to her chamber. Through the assistance of the kind court matron who recognized their pure fidelity, the lovers were brought before the Caliph.

Instead of ordering their execution, the Caliph Abd al-Malik was deeply touched by Ni'amah’s fearless journey across the desert and Naomi’s unwavering fidelity. The Caliph bestowed royal gifts upon them, granted them a magnificent mansion in Kufa, and praised their enduring devotion as an example for all his realm.
moral: Steadfast loyalty, courteous resourcefulness, and mutual respect conquer the most formidable fortresses.
